learningObjective: Enumerate boundary conditions that block or complicate operator fusion in a deep-learning compiler.

canonicalClaims.claim: Fusion is blocked when producer and consumer are on different devices, because a data-transfer op cannot be absorbed into a single device kernel.
conditions: IR carries explicit device placement attributes.
The transfer op is not a no-op (e.g., not a UMA / unified-memory identity).
nonImplications: Does not imply cross-device pipelines cannot be fused within each device.

canonicalClaims.claim: Fusion across a mutation that is aliased by a live consumer would reorder observable reads/writes and is thus illegal.
conditions: Alias analysis identifies the shared storage.
The mutating op has a live down-stream consumer of the pre-mutation value.
nonImplications: Does not imply all in-place ops block fusion; when no live consumer observes the pre-mutation value, fusion may proceed.

canonicalClaims.claim: Explicit graph outputs must be materialized; fusion cannot remove their materialization without changing the observable API contract.
conditions: Output tensor is on the return signature of the compiled graph.
nonImplications: Does not imply the compiler cannot fuse into a producer of the output; only that the output tensor itself must exist post-fusion.

misconceptions.claim: Different iteration-space ranks (e.g., pointwise → reduction) form a hard fusion boundary.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Pointwise→reduction fusion is a standard pattern (e.g., LayerNorm, softmax). Rank differences complicate scheduling but do not block legality.

misconceptions.claim: FP32 accumulation makes fusion illegal because register pressure always grows unboundedly.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Accumulator dtype is a numerical choice; register pressure is a performance heuristic, not a legality boundary.

misconceptions.claim: Pointwise-pointwise fusion is disallowed because both ops share the same iteration space.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Shared iteration space is exactly what makes pointwise-pointwise fusion the most trivial and common fusion pattern.

misconceptions.claim: Fusion boundaries are purely a performance concern, not a legality concern.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Some boundaries (device placement, aliased mutation, explicit outputs) are legality conditions; others (register pressure) are performance heuristics.

implementationFacts: TVM Relax marks ops with opacity levels (kInjective, kReduction, kOpaque) to drive fusion.
TorchInductor tracks mutation via functionalization and refuses to fuse across live-aliased writes.
performanceScenarios: A CPU-loaded tensor followed by a GPU pointwise op requires an H2D copy, forming an unavoidable fusion boundary.
